short: The five human TFAP2 proteins (TFAP2A-E, historically AP-2 alpha through epsilon) bind a pseudo-palindrome made of GCC and GGC triplets separated by exactly three bases. Each subunit contributes a basic region that inserts a loop into the major groove, and the two subunits are held together by a helix-span-helix domain; the factors are constitutive dimers even off DNA, and all paralogue combinations heterodimerize. The site is GC-rich and sits in GC-rich promoters and neural crest enhancers. TFAP2 factors behave as pioneer factors during neural crest specification, and mutations cause branchio-oculo-facial syndrome (TFAP2A) and Char syndrome (TFAP2B). A hit identifies the family, not a paralogue.
long:
## The factors

Five human genes encode this family: TFAP2A, TFAP2B, TFAP2C, TFAP2D and TFAP2E, still widely
called AP-2 alpha, beta, gamma, delta and epsilon. Each protein has an N-terminal proline- and
glutamine-rich activation domain [PMID:3063603,2010091], a basic region, and a C-terminal helix-span-helix (HSH)
dimerization domain: two amphipathic helices separated by a long span. The HSH domain drives
dimerization on its own and can be transplanted onto a foreign basic region, but it cannot bind
DNA without an adjacent basic region [PMID:1998122]. AP-2 is a dimer in solution as well as on DNA [PMID:2010091], and all of
the paralogue pairs can heterodimerize; in neural crest development TFAP2A switches partners from
TFAP2C to TFAP2B as specification proceeds, and the two heterodimers open different sets of
elements [PMID:31848212]. Expression is restricted rather than housekeeping: TFAP2A and TFAP2B in neural crest,
surface ectoderm, facial mesenchyme and kidney [PMID:1989904]; TFAP2C in trophoblast, germ cells and luminal
breast epithelium; TFAP2D mainly in retina and midbrain; TFAP2E in olfactory epithelium. TFAP2D
is the outlier, with a divergent basic region and weaker transactivation.

## The motif

The functional element is a pseudo-palindrome of two triplets, GCC and GGC, with a three-base
spacer: GCC(N3)GGC [PMID:37409559]. SELEX with AP-2 alpha also recovered GCC(N4)GGC and GCC(N3/4)GGG
sites [PMID:10373594], and the older consensus GCCYGCRGGC is an N4 form. The database 9-mers (GCCTGAGGC,
GCCTCAGGC) are N3; the longer models are not that core plus flanks, since the extra C and G sit inside
the triplets: GCCCYAGGGC is GCC(N4)GGC, and GCCCTBAGGGC reads as GCC(N4)GGG. The data consensus,
GCCTCAGGGCA, is a longer form (GCC(N4)GGC, or GCC(N3)GGG), so it differs from the literature's
GCC(N3)GGC in spacing, not only in flanks.
The crystal structure of the TFAP2A DBD-HSH tandem domain on DNA explains the geometry: the two
flat amphipathic HSH helices stack against each other through hydrophobic contacts, and a
stabilized loop from each DBD inserts into one of two neighboring major grooves [PMID:37409559]. Because the two
loops are a fixed distance apart, spacer length, not just spacer sequence, determines binding: a
three-base gap is strongly preferred: TFAP2A bound a four-base spacer about 18-fold more weakly and two-
or five-base spacers barely at all [PMID:37409559]. This makes the informative
positions the GCC and GGC triplets, with the central three bases nearly free (commonly written
YAG or TCA/TGA). The five paralogues are not separable from sequence. Every model in this family's
data carries the same GCC and GGC/GGG triplets (7.5-14.5 bits); they differ in spacer length, but
TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C each have models of more than one spacing.

## Where it acts

AP-2 sites are GC-rich, so they are enriched in GC-rich and CpG-island promoters, where they can
be hard to distinguish from SP/KLF GC-boxes on loose models. The functionally important sites,
however, are largely distal: TFAP2A occupies thousands of enhancers at the neural plate border and
in specified neural crest, acting as a pioneer factor that remodels chromatin ahead of the
lineage program [PMID:31848212]. In melanocytes TFAP2 paralogues bind in parallel with MITF at pigmentation genes [PMID:28249010].
In luminal breast cancer cells TFAP2C co-occupies enhancers with estrogen receptor and FOXA1 and
regulates ESR1 itself [PMID:24469049]. Co-occurring motifs therefore depend on the tissue: SOX and PAX motifs in
neural crest, MITF E-boxes in melanocytes, ERE and forkhead sites in breast. AP-2 sites are common
enough in GC-rich sequence that a genome-wide scan returns very large numbers of matches; the
constraint on real occupancy is TFAP2 expression, which is narrow.

## Biology and disease

Tfap2a-null mice fail cranial neural tube closure and have severe craniofacial defects, matching
AP-2's expression in ectoderm and migrating cranial neural crest [PMID:8622765,1989904]. In humans, heterozygous TFAP2A
mutations, mostly missense changes in the basic region and HSH domain, cause branchio-oculo-facial
syndrome: cervical and infra-auricular skin defects, ocular anomalies, cleft lip or palate, and
sometimes inner ear malformation and deafness [PMID:18423521]. Mutations in TFAP2B cause Char syndrome, a dominant
condition combining patent ductus arteriosus, a distinctive face and hand anomalies, with a
genotype-phenotype relationship that tracks with how much DNA binding is lost [PMID:10802654]. TFAP2C is amplified
and overexpressed in a subset of breast cancers, where it governs the luminal epithelial phenotype
and hormone response and higher expression predicts worse outcome on anti-hormonal therapy [PMID:24469049].
TFAP2A and TFAP2C are also required in trophoblast and germ cell programs. A structural survey of
disease mutations concluded that reduced or abolished DNA binding is the primary mechanism in
TFAP2-associated disease [PMID:37409559].

## Reading a hit

A GCC(N3)GGC match tells you that a TFAP2 dimer could bind, and nothing about which one. The five
paralogues share one matrix; assign a member from expression, and remember that the biologically
active species is often a heterodimer, so the question may have no single answer. Check the spacer
before believing a match: two bases is a poor site, while four binds more weakly than three in vitro
but was recovered by SELEX and is common in the models here, so it is weaker evidence, not a non-site
[PMID:37409559,10373594]. Permissive scanners report all of these spacings. Because
the site is GC-rich, the main false-positive risk is confusion with other GC-binding families. A
loose AP-2 model will score on SP1/KLF GC-boxes (GGGGCGGGG) and on CpG-island sequence generally;
conversely, GC-box models score on AP-2 sites. Require the discontinuous GCC...GGC arrangement
rather than a continuous GC run before calling a hit AP-2. The evidence base here is comparatively
clean: HOCOMOCO models for AP2A and AP2C are grade A with combined ChIP-seq and in vitro selection
(PSM), and the AP2B and AP2E models rest on in vitro selection alone (SM), so the family's
specificity does not depend on ChIP data. The one provenance caveat is the CIS-BP TFAP2D entry,
which is transferred from a mouse protein at 80% DNA-binding-domain identity [PMID:25215497].
caveats: All five TFAP2 paralogues share one matrix and heterodimerize freely, so a hit identifies the family only. Spacer length is part of the motif: three bases is the canonical, tightest-binding form, four is weaker but was recovered by selection and appears in many models here, and two is a poor site. The biggest practical risk is GC-richness. AP-2 models cross-score with SP/KLF GC-boxes and with CpG-island sequence, so a GC-rich promoter hit needs the discontinuous GCC...GGC arrangement to be credible. Genome-wide matches vastly outnumber occupied sites because TFAP2 expression is narrow. In vitro evidence supports the core specificity; the CIS-BP TFAP2D model is inferred from mouse at 80% domain identity.

timeline.finding: Cloning of human AP-2, a factor that binds inducible viral and cellular enhancers, reveals a DNA-binding region unlike any known motif and a proline- and glutamine-rich activation region.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning, bacterial expression, in vitro transcription, transfection
timeline.open: How a protein with no recognizable DNA-binding motif contacted DNA.

timeline.finding: AP-2 binds a palindromic site as a dimer and is dimeric even without DNA; sequence-specific binding needs a helix-span-helix dimerization domain plus an adjacent basic region, and the HSH domain can drive DNA binding by the c-Jun basic region.
timeline.methods: DNA contact studies, cross-linking, deletion mutants, domain-swap chimeras

timeline.finding: AP-2-null mice die perinatally with failed cranial neural tube closure and severe malformations of face, skull, sensory organs and cranial ganglia.

SELEX and missing-phosphate analysis of AP-2 alpha show a flexible protein-DNA complex that accepts three related site classes, GCC N3 GGC, GCC N4 GGC and GCC N3/4 GGG, rather than a single fixed spacing.
timeline.methods: SELEX, missing-phosphate and nucleotide competition analysis
timeline.open: Which site class predominates in cells, and whether the paralogues differ in it.

timeline.finding: Missense TFAP2B mutations cause Char syndrome; the mutant proteins dimerize normally but bind the TFAP2 site abnormally and act as dominant negatives, the first human TFAP2 disease.
timeline.methods: Positional candidate cloning, in vitro binding and transactivation assays

timeline.finding: During neural crest development TFAP2A acts as a pioneer factor whose genomic targets depend on its partner: TFAP2A/C heterodimers at the neural plate border, then TFAP2A/B heterodimers during crest specification.
timeline.methods: Genomic occupancy and chromatin-state profiling, loss of function
timeline.open: Whether heterodimers differ in sequence preference or only in where they are expressed.

timeline.finding: Structures of the TFAP2A DBD-HSH tandem on DNA show the stacked HSH helices fixing two DBD loops in adjacent major grooves, so both the GCC/GGC triplets and the spacer length set specificity; disease mutations act mainly by reducing DNA binding.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography, binding assays with spacer variants, mutant analysis
timeline.open: How the strict-spacer model accommodates the N4 and GGG-type sites selected in 1999.

open: How strict the spacer is remains disputed: the 2023 TFAP2A structure and binding data favor a fixed three-base spacer, while 1999 SELEX with AP-2 alpha recovered GCC N4 GGC and GCC N3/4 GGG sites as well, and the extended database models (GCCCTBAGGGC) read as GCC N4 GGG rather than GCC N3 GGC.

Whether TFAP2 heterodimers differ in DNA specificity is unknown: TFAP2A/B and TFAP2A/C heterodimers occupy different elements in neural crest, but every measured paralogue model is the same matrix, so the difference may come from partner availability and chromatin rather than sequence.
TFAP2D has a divergent basic region, yet its only model here is inferred from a mouse protein at 80% domain identity, so whether TFAP2D shares the family specificity has not been measured.
